prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based therapy for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings put B042 first, but agreement on ranking is not itself evidence of merit, so I restate the case. The arc runs from the incretin effect and proglucagon processing, through identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide and its insulinotropic and satiety actions, to receptor biology and long-acting agonists with randomized evidence of benefit on weight, glycaemia and now cardiovascular and renal outcomes. It is a rare case in which the physiology is clear, the discovery is original, independent confirmation spans decades, and the clinical consequence is very large. On maturity there is no real argument for waiting. I keep Drucker, Holst and Mojsov because that trio best fits a prize for discovery, which is the Nobel Committee's usual emphasis, and because it covers the hormone's identification, physiology and biology.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Three names cannot cover Holst, Drucker, Mojsov, Knudsen and other early peptide contributors such as Habener who are outside the credited list, and Mojsov's priority is contested in public accounts. Excluding Knudsen means the prize honours the biology and not the drugs that changed practice. Some may see that as an incomplete reading of 'incretin-based therapy'. I also rely on recollection of the historical record for priority details, and the supplied files do not let me verify it. If the committee cannot reach a defensible allocation, B033 is the cleanest fallback: Walter and Mori form a compact, widely accepted pair, but with weaker direct clinical payoff.

responses.point: Linnarsson argues that Drucker, Holst and Mojsov are the most defensible three because Knudsen is a drug-development figure whose scientific discovery credit is better held by the others. He also ranked B006 second and B045 fourth.
responses.response: I agree with the trio and reach it by the same reasoning, but I want to qualify it. Drug development is not automatically second-tier, and the physiology-to-therapy arc is what makes this candidate stronger than any other on the shortlist. I am excluding Knudsen because of the three-name cap, not because her contribution is lesser, and I would want the citation to say so openly. I disagree with ranking B006 above B049. Allocation among Hall, Schreiber and Sabatini is unresolved, and the rapalog clinical payoff is modest. A shortlist position for mTOR does not reduce the attribution problem.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks B042 first with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. He treats Knudsen as the necessary development leg and regards the exclusion of Mojsov as a forced and difficult choice.
responses.response: This is the main real disagreement on B042, and I find his version coherent. If the committee wants the prize to honour the translation of the discovery into therapy, Knudsen is stronger than Mojsov. I weigh it the other way because the prize cites discovery, and Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active peptide is the step from which the physiology becomes usable. The cost of his version is that Mojsov, whose credit is debated but real, is omitted. I would accept either trio as a legitimate majority outcome. I would not accept a configuration whose citation implies that the discovery history is settled when it is not.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius sees Holst and Drucker as the clearest scientific anchors, says Mojsov's credit is real but debated and cannot be adjudicated from the files, and ranks B033 second ahead of B049.
responses.response: I agree that Holst and Drucker are the anchors and that the Mojsov question cannot be settled from the supplied evidence. We propose the same trio, but I would be firmer about the third seat. Identification and synthesis of the active peptide is the technical step that made GLP-1 pharmacology possible, so I find her case stronger than that of any uncredited contributor, while accepting that the citation should not imply the priority history is settled. I also agree that B033 is a clean second option, which is why it is my first alternative.

responses.point: Svenningsson, who chairs, regards a biology-centred three-person prize as feasible but notes that it omits Knudsen and others, and he ranks B049 and B027 above B033.
responses.response: I accept that the allocation problem is real. My ranking differs on B033 and B049 only in order. Both are strong, and I would defend either as a distinct second prize part if the union fits within three people. B027 is attractive to me for its mechanistic clarity, but I rank it lower because it is a single-disease success and its therapeutic platform is younger than the leading candidates. On B049 I would still want Eshhar's first-generation CAR work addressed before accepting a trio.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to credit the discovery of GLP-1 physiology (Holst, Drucker, Mojsov) or to include drug development (Knudsen) within the three-person limit.
Priority between Mojsov, Habener and others for identification of the active GLP-1 peptide is not verifiable from the supplied files.
Whether pairing B042 with a second achievement is worthwhile, since the three-person cap leaves little room beyond a GLP-1 trio.
How much weight the committee gives to the absence of a direct clinical payoff in B033 compared with the diffuse attribution in B049.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal issue is apparent for any shortlisted candidate. My profile documents joint publications with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisen, and with Christopher Burge's group at MIT, but none of them is credited on a shortlisted ballot. KI is also a shared institution. Smart-seq methods and single-cell RNA work are not on the shortlist.
